html:
A British government plan of 1946 to grow peanuts (groundnuts) on a huge scale in Tanganyika, then a British-run territory, to ease Britain's postwar shortage of cooking fat and margarine. It was abandoned in 1951 as a costly failure.

The Attlee government put the plan in the hands of the state's Overseas Food Corporation. Planners in London chose land at Kongwa and other sites without proper soil or rainfall surveys. Surplus army tractors and bulldozers were shipped in to clear the bush, and broke down on roots and hard clay. Droughts came, the soil baked hard, and in some years the harvest was smaller than the seed planted.

The scheme lost tens of millions of pounds, a great sum at the time. It became a byword for large, top-down development planned far from the place it was meant to help, along with other colonial projects such as the Office du Niger. Some cleared land was later used for cattle ranching and other crops.
